messages.author: 7942473998baeb45
messages.subject: FIRMA Scores
parts:
Hi everyone,

I have some exon arrays which I am analysing to determine alternative
splicing. I have been able to obtain FIRMA scores for my data but I am
unsure as to how to proceed from here.
How are these scores to be interpreted, intuitively and statistically?
Which algorithm is used to calculate them?
Also if I wish to look for alt splicing between two of my 4 treatments
what steps should I now take?
Is there some example code or documentation on FIRMA scores which I
could look at?

Thanks for your time,

Jason

messages.author: 1ff63ac4948de366
messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] FIRMA Scores
parts:
Hi Jason.

Many of your questions will be answered when the FIRMA paper comes
out, which'll hopefully be soon (the revision is being resubmitted
next week I think).

But, basically, you are looking for large-in-magnitude FIRMA scores,
so high positive or high negative. FIRMA scores are summaries of the
residuals (default: median) by probeset after a robust RMA model
fit ... for a given gene. Statistical interpretation of FIRMA scores
is still somewhat of an open question, but they are at least on a
normalized scale and so should be comparable across genes ... and/or
you should be able to look at the distribution of FIRMA scores and
look for ones that stand out.

As for looking across groups/treatments, I usually do the simplistic
thing of using limma directly on the FIRMA scores and looking for
differences between groups. That certainly has highlighted some
interesting genes for me.

Note: I/we have found it fairly important to look at the probe-level
data in combination with the residuals and FIRMA scores, as there are
specific cases where large residuals can be misleading.

I have a few scripts that might be useful to you. Elizabeth might
have some ready-made ones also.

Hope that helps.
Mark

messages.author: 43e2e19dd6bd2992
messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: FIRMA Scores
parts:
Hi Jason,
It depends what you mean as necessary. As Mark says, for a certain
analysis we did the normalization and BG correction on all of the
main-design probes and then switched to the Ensbl to do the probe-level
model. So it's optional, in the sense that you could use the Ensbl cdf
from the beginning; the main reason we didn't do that was that then only
probes that are in that cdf are normalized and BG corrected, so if you
wanted to look at additional probes they wouldn't be corrected values.
So that depends on your analysis whether it's important to you.

But another question you might be asking is whether you could just stick
with the main design cdf for the entire analysis. Technically you *can*
(obviously) but it would not be recommended by us. The algorithm will be
very much thrown off by the level of non-expressed probesets that would
be added to any particular gene/transcript cluster. This is true also
for Affymetrix's algorithm(s). The reasons are multiple, but one reason
is that adding all of the non-expressed probesets available in the main
design would break any robust fitting algorithm (like RMA's or Affy's
Plier) to be able to do this -- and your chip effect estimates would be
lousy. The other reason, which is more important, is that the algorithm
assumes that unless the probeset is alternatively expressed, the
expression levels of the chips are parallel across probes -- the
different probe affinities only cause linear shifts (this is the linear
model fit by RMA); probesets that as a whole don't do this are called
alternatively expressed. But the non-expressed probesets generally will
have a very different behavior than the expressed probesets and so will
be called as alternatively spliced: lots of false positives. The better
your annotation, the less false positives this will give.

However, if you are just getting probeset estimates (mergeGroups=FALSE)
from the linear fitting then you can use the main-design cdf all the way
through.

On the otherhand, if you like having Affy's transcript clusters, you
could use the 'core' probesets and probably do okay. We like the Ensembl
cdf better because how Affy clusters probesets together results in
stringing a some genes together, while we tend to throw more of those
out, I think (as well as noting when they occur in the names we give the
unit. Ultimately we found it easier to stick to one carefully done
annotation; while core are 'reliable' probesets, they are still from
multiple sources which are combined together algorithmically by Affy.
Even combining RefSeq transcripts (a main annotation in core) into gene
definitions seems difficult, based on talking to someone who did it,
while Ensembl is more straightforward.

Best,
Elizabeth

messages.subject: Re: FIRMA Scores
parts:
Hi everyone,

I'm pretty new in the 'exon-array-business' so hopefully my questions
won't be too stupid...

I'm using your software for some weeks now trying to get some
information about alternative splicing out of my eight chips (2 groups
with four chips each). As far as the fit-plm-step everything seems
logical to me and I can fairly understand it. By then some questions
arise:

(1) Is there any information (besides the paper) available by now
about how FIRMA works or how to interpret the scores? How can I do a
statistical hypothesis test based on the the scores?

(2) The FirmaModel()-routine requires an object of ExonRmaPlm class
and fit() then calculates a score by exon for every array. So how do I
have to create this ExonRmaPlm-object? Do I have to use
... <- ExonRmaPlm(..., mergeGroups=TRUE,...) #treat all exons
separately, only group probes
or
... <- ExonRmaPlm(..., mergeGroups=FALSE,...) #merge exons into
transcripts
I suppose one could do it both ways, but which one is the more
reasonable?

(3) Since Firma calculates the score by array you should somehow merge
these values to get a score by group. Is it a good idea to simply use
the mean?

(4) What is about filtering? The Affymetrix technical note
http://www.affymetrix.com/support/technical/technotes/id_altsplicingevents_technote.pdf
suggests several steps of filtering. Is this all done by fitting the
FirmaModel? I don't see any arguments for filtering in the fit()-
method...?

(5) Is the Firma-score in any way comparable to the Splicing Index
Value?

(6) Suppose I would like to calculate a Splicing Index by myself, is
it a good idea to do something like this (as draft):
... # background correction + quantile normalization with
core-cdfs yields csN
cdfEnsb <- AffymetrixCdfFile$fromChipType(paste(chipType, "U-
Ensembl47,G-Affy", sep=","))
setCdf(csN, cdfEnsb)
plmExon <- ExonRmaPlm(csN,
mergeGroups=FALSE,tag=c("*","ensb")) # contains probe set
intensities
plmTranscript <- ExonRmaPlm(csN,
mergeGroups=TRUE,tag=c("*","ensb")) # contains transcript cluster
intensities (right?)
# all intensities should be stored as 2^x, even though the ExonRmaPlm
doesn't inherit from AffymetrixCelSet...? Right?
"pick an exonXY"
splicing index of exonXY <- log2("exonXY intensity from
plmExon" / "intensity of transcript cluster containing exonXY from
plmTranscript")


I hope you can help me out with some of my questions. Thanks a lot in
advance,
Frank

> information about alternative splicing out of my eight chips (2 groups
> with four chips each). As far as the fit-plm-step everything seems
> logical to me and I can fairly understand it. By then some questions
> arise:
>
> (1) Is there any information (besides the paper) available by now
> about how FIRMA works or how to interpret the scores? How can I do a
> statistical hypothesis test based on the the scores?

Generally, potential differential splice events are associated with
'extreme' FIRMA scores (i.e. large positive or large negative). In
your case, you may be looking for differences between your 2 groups.
In the past, I have done a 'limma' analysis to look for differences
between 2 groups, operating directly on FIRMA scores.

> (2) The FirmaModel()-routine requires an object of ExonRmaPlm class
> and fit() then calculates a score by exon for every array. So how do I
> have to create this ExonRmaPlm-object? Do I have to use
> ... <- ExonRmaPlm(..., mergeGroups=TRUE,...) #treat all exons
> separately, only group probes
> or
> ... <- ExonRmaPlm(..., mergeGroups=FALSE,...) #merge exons into
> transcripts
> I suppose one could do it both ways, but which one is the more
> reasonable?

I think you have the mergeGroups logic the wrong way around.
mergeGroups=TRUE for gene-level summaries, mergeGroups=FALSE for
probeset (~exon)-level summaries. For input to FIRMA, you'll want
mergeGroups=TRUE since FIRMA operates on the residuals from a gene-
level fit.

> (3) Since Firma calculates the score by array you should somehow merge
> these values to get a score by group. Is it a good idea to simply use
> the mean?

Depends how heterogeneous your samples are and how conservative you
want to me. Like I said above, maybe a 'limma' analysis or something
similar would be helpful to find differences in FIRMA scores between
groups.

> (4) What is about filtering? The Affymetrix technical note
> http://www.affymetrix.com/support/technical/technotes/
> id_altsplicingevents_technote.pdf
> suggests several steps of filtering. Is this all done by fitting the
> FirmaModel? I don't see any arguments for filtering in the fit()-
> method...?

I haven't done too much filtering in my analyses so far. I do,
however, have a look at the probe-level data and the residuals to try
and get an idea of what is happening. FirmaModel does not do
filtering. One thing I would be wary of is FIRMA scores that come
from 1 or 2 probes. Most probesets have 4 probes, but extreme FIRMA
scores that come from probesets with 1 or 2 probes might be either
worth filtering out or just considering differently.

> (5) Is the Firma-score in any way comparable to the Splicing Index
> Value?

When the paper comes out, there is more description of this. They
are not directly comparable, but generally have a positive association.

> (6) Suppose I would like to calculate a Splicing Index by myself, is
> it a good idea to do something like this (as draft):
> ... # background correction + quantile normalization with
> core-cdfs yields csN
> cdfEnsb <- AffymetrixCdfFile$fromChipType(paste(chipType, "U-
> Ensembl47,G-Affy", sep=","))
> setCdf(csN, cdfEnsb)
> plmExon <- ExonRmaPlm(csN,
> mergeGroups=FALSE,tag=c("*","ensb")) # contains probe set
> intensities
> plmTranscript <- ExonRmaPlm(csN,
> mergeGroups=TRUE,tag=c("*","ensb")) # contains transcript cluster
> intensities (right?)
> # all intensities should be stored as 2^x, even though the ExonRmaPlm
> doesn't inherit from AffymetrixCelSet...? Right?
> "pick an exonXY"
> splicing index of exonXY <- log2("exonXY intensity from
> plmExon" / "intensity of transcript cluster containing exonXY from
> plmTranscript")

Elizabeth may have some code for this, but this looks reasonably
close to what you want ... after the fitting and extracting
intensities, etc. ExonRmaPlm doesn't inherit from AffymetrixCelSet
but ChipEffectSet does, which is what will contain the chip effects
that you will need. So, yes, the intensities that you extract will
be on 2^x. The mergeGroups is the correct way around here.

Hope that is helpful.

Cheers,
Mark

[4] "AffymetrixFileSet" "GenericDataFileSet" "Object"

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] FIRMA Scores
parts:
Hi Maria.

I've copied the group list in case others have this same question.

Assuming you've done some standard processing, here is a possible
backend ...

plmTr <- ExonRmaPlm(csN, mergeGroups=TRUE)
fit(plmTr, verbose=verbose)

rs <- calculateResiduals(plmTr, verbose=verbose)
firma <- FirmaModel(plmTr)
fit(firma, verbose=verbose)
fs <- getFirmaScores(firma)

exFirma <- extractDataFrame(fs,addNames=TRUE)
exFirma[,6:ncol(exFirma)]<-log2(exFirma[,6:ncol(exFirma)])

.... here what I'd suggest is running 'limma' on your FIRMA scores to
highlight differences in your replicated groups ... so consult some
real examples as I'm just doing this on the top of my head ...

library(limma)
fit<-lmFit(exFirma[,6:ncol(exFirma)], model.matrix(~
your.class.variable))
fit<-eBayes(fit)

topTable(fit) ... should highlight some top probesets if there are
any ...

One thing to keep in mind is the number of probes per probeset ...
sometimes you can get some fairly extreme FIRMA scores for probesets
with just 1 or 2 probes. I would suggest removing probesets with
only 1 or 2 probes (or at least treating them differently).

To do this, you can find

nProbesPerExon<-readCdfNbrOfCellsPerUnitGroup(getPathname(cdf))
nProbesPerExonVector<-unlist(nProbesPerExon)

(this should be a vector of the same length as the number of rows of
exFirma above).

I'm planning to put this all in a vignette, but I haven't been able to
finish it yet ...

Cheers,
Mark
